issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only when the trial court’s view is clearly unreasonable or perverse and substantial and compelling reasons justify intervention.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the appellant, but the High Court convicted him on the State’s appeal against acquittal.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s assessment perverse and unreasonable, including its rejection of credible eyewitness evidence and its reliance on extraneous matters.
The Supreme Court found reliable evidence implicating the appellant and held that there were compelling and substantial reasons for the High Court to interfere.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reverse the acquittal, and the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: An acquittal strengthens the presumption of innocence. An appellate court should not disturb a reasonably possible view merely because another view is possible; it may intervene where the acquittal is clearly unreasonable or perverse and substantial and compelling reasons require intervention to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and (trial_view_is_perverse or trial_view_is_clearly_unreasonable) and substantial_reasons_for_intervention

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_is_perverse: The trial court reached its view through serious errors in assessing the evidence or by relying on matters that should not determine the case.
predicates.trial_view_is_clearly_unreasonable: The trial court’s view is not a reasonable view of the evidence.
predicates.substantial_reasons_for_intervention: The evidence and circumstances provide substantial and compelling reasons to intervene to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the acquittal may be reversed if the trial court’s view is perverse or clearly unreasonable and substantial reasons support intervention.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence from an interested witness is not inherently unreliable, and corroboration is not invariably required if the testimony remains convincing after careful scrutiny.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses were related to the deceased or otherwise said to be interested, and there was enmity between the families.
The Supreme Court scrutinized their evidence and found the testimony of the eyewitness and the supporting witnesses acceptable.
The eyewitness account was also supported by the evidence of witnesses who saw the accused leave with weapons and by other circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship or interest did not make their evidence inadmissible or unusable; the evidence could be relied upon after careful scrutiny, with corroboration available in this case.
issues.legal_principle: As stated in Raju @ Balachandran & Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2012) 12 SCC 701, interested-witness evidence must be carefully scrutinized. Such evidence is not infirm merely because of the witness’s interest, and corroboration is a matter of prudence rather than an absolute requirement where the testimony is intrinsically good.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and witness_has_interest_in_outcome and testimony_survives_careful_scrutiny and testimony_is_intrinsically_reliable

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which witness testimony is being assessed.
predicates.witness_has_interest_in_outcome: The witness has a relationship, stake, or enmity that may give the witness an interest in the outcome.
predicates.testimony_survives_careful_scrutiny: The court has closely examined the witness’s testimony and found it credible despite the claimed interest.
predicates.testimony_is_intrinsically_reliable: The testimony is convincing in itself and is not rendered unreliable by its content or circumstances.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, interested-witness evidence may be relied on when careful scrutiny leaves the testimony intrinsically reliable.

issues.legal_issue: A credible eyewitness who had an adequate opportunity to observe the accused may identify them despite darkness or the witness’s status as a pardanashin woman.
material_facts: The eyewitness was beside her husband when the assailants entered and was close to them during the attack and their departure.
She saw the assailants in torchlight, including when they turned and looked at her, and knew the appellant from the same family and locality.
Her account was consistent with the injuries and was supported by evidence that the appellant left carrying a weapon.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness had an adequate opportunity to see and identify the appellant, and the challenge to her identification was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed identification by considering the witness’s opportunity to observe, proximity, lighting, and prior familiarity. It rejected the proposition that a pardanashin woman could not identify men merely because she was pardanashin; the evidence showed that she had seen them at close quarters in torchlight.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and eyewitness_testimony and adequate_opportunity_to_observe and identification_supported_by_familiarity_or_observation_conditions

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the identity of an accused is disputed.
predicates.eyewitness_testimony: A witness claims to have personally seen the relevant incident or the accused involved in it.
predicates.adequate_opportunity_to_observe: The witness was close enough and had sufficient time or suitable conditions to see the accused.
predicates.identification_supported_by_familiarity_: The witness knew the accused or the circumstances of observation, such as available light, support identification.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, an eyewitness’s identification may be accepted when the witness had an adequate opportunity to observe and familiarity or the observation conditions support identification.

issues.legal_issue: Absence of motive does not undermine a prosecution case supported by reliable eyewitness testimony.
material_facts: The defence argued that the appellant lacked a motive to kill the deceased.
The court found evidence of strained relations between the families and held that motive was not absent.
The court also found the eyewitness account reliable and supported by other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The argument based on absence of motive was rejected; in any event, reliable eyewitness evidence makes absence of motive insignificant.
issues.legal_principle: Where reliable eyewitness evidence establishes involvement in an offence, absence of motive pales into insignificance. The court also found motive on the facts, including strained relations and disputes between the families.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.reliable_eyewitness_account: A credible eyewitness account supports the accused’s involvement in the offence.
predicates.motive_is_absent: The prosecution has not established a reason for the accused to commit the offence.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, the absence of motive does not defeat the prosecution case when a reliable eyewitness account supports it.

issues.legal_issue: An alibi is not established when the accused provides no evidence supporting the claim that they were elsewhere at the time of the offence.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that he was away preparing his thesis and was not present in the village on the night of the offence.
He produced no evidence that he was staying elsewhere, and there was no evidence about the distance between his educational institution and the village.
The Supreme Court held that the alibi plea was not proved.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s alibi plea was rejected as unproved.
issues.legal_principle: A bare assertion of absence from the scene does not establish an alibi; the court assessed the claim against the absence of supporting evidence and found it unproved.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the accused’s presence at the relevant place and time is in issue.
predicates.accused_claims_presence_elsewhere: The accused asserts that they were somewhere other than the scene when the offence occurred.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_claimed_absence: The accused provides no evidence supporting the assertion of presence elsewhere.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, an alibi is not established when the accused claims to have been elsewhere but provides no supporting evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding a criminal case must not treat case-diary entries or general public opinion as proof of guilt or innocence.
material_facts: The trial court relied on an investigating officer’s case-diary entry recording a general belief that accused persons other than one accused had been falsely implicated.
The Supreme Court held that reliance on such diary entries was impermissible and that general public feeling had no relevance to deciding the case.
The court stated that the decision must rest on legal evidence adduced before the court.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s reliance on the diary entry and general public opinion was a gross error of law and contributed to the perversity of its acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mohd Ankoos & Ors. v. Public Prosecutor, High Court of A.P., Hyderabad, (2010) 1 SCC 94, and Shamshul Kanwar v. State of U.P., (1995) 4 SCC 430, reliance on case-diary entries of this kind is not permissible. A criminal court must decide on legal evidence adduced before it, not general public opinion.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case decided by a court.
predicates.court_relies_on_case_diary_or_public_opi: The court treats an investigative diary entry or general public belief as proof in deciding the case.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, treating case-diary material or general public opinion as proof is impermissible.
